Eliada
ē-lī´ă-dah
n. (a son of David; also the father of a Syrian adversary and a Benjamite captain)
Hebrew Elyada, meaning God knows or God has known. The Chronicler preserves a variant, Beeliada, and notes the equivalence in the margin — a name changed to purge the syllable Baal from it.

Biblical Definition

He appears in the list of sons born to David at Jerusalem: “And Elishama, and Eliada, and Eliphalet” (2 Samuel 5:16). The Chronicler gives the same three: “And Elishama, and Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine” (1 Chronicles 3:8). But in another place the Chronicler records the older form of the name: “And Elishama, and Beeliada, and Eliphalet” (1 Chronicles 14:7) — Beeliada, meaning Baal knows. The same substitution appears elsewhere in Scripture: Ishbosheth was originally Eshbaal, and Mephibosheth was Meribbaal. As Israel came to understand what the Baal cult was, names built on that syllable were revised. Hosea records the LORD Himself announcing the change: “And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali” (Hosea 2:16). The Hebrew baal simply means lord or husband, and was once used innocently; when it had been thoroughly claimed by an idol, God would not be addressed by it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Eliada; the Hebrew signifies God knows, and the name belongs to a son of David and to others.

expand to see more

ELIADA, n. A son of David born in Jerusalem; in Hebrew, God knows.

BAAL, n. The chief male deity of the Phoenicians and Canaanites; in Hebrew, a lord, master, husband or possessor.

ISHI, n. In Hebrew, my husband; the title by which the LORD would be called instead of Baali.

EUPHEMISM, n. A figure of speech in which a harsh or offensive word is replaced by a milder one.

SYNCRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance.

2 Samuel 5:16 — "And Elishama, and Eliada, and Eliphalet."

1 Chronicles 3:8 — "And Elishama, and Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine."

Hosea 2:16 — "And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali."

Modern Corruption

Borrowed religious vocabulary is defended as harmless on the ground that words are neutral, when Scripture shows God retiring a term that a rival worship had captured.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that words can be taken captive. Baal began as an ordinary Hebrew word for lord or husband, and Israelites used it in their children's names without any thought of the Canaanite storm-god. By Hosea's day the syllable had been so thoroughly annexed by an idol that the LORD announced He would no longer be addressed by it: thou shalt call me Ishi, and shalt call me no more Baali. The name Beeliada became Eliada, and Eshbaal became Ishbosheth, for the same reason.

The application is not that Christians should police vocabulary anxiously, but that they should notice when a word has changed owners. Much of the difficulty in modern theological argument is that terms both parties use — love, justice, inclusion, identity, even grace — have been redefined by a rival framework while keeping their old warmth. Hosea's remedy was not a campaign against a syllable but a change of address that made the object of worship unmistakable. Where a term can no longer be used without importing an alien meaning, the faithful course is to say plainly what is meant, as God did.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Elyada (H450), God knows; Beelyada (H1182), Baal knows; baal (H1167), lord, husband, owner; ishi (H376), my husband.

expand to see more

Hebrew Elyada (H450) — God knows; a son of David born at Jerusalem.

Hebrew Beelyada (H1182) — Baal knows; the older form in 1 Chronicles 14:7.

Hebrew baal (H1167) — lord, master, husband, owner; and the name of the idol.

Hebrew ishi (H376) — my man, my husband; the title Hosea 2:16 substitutes.

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; the verb at the heart of the name.

Usage

"“Elishama, and Eliada, and Eliphalet” — the sons born in Jerusalem."

"“Elishama, and Beeliada, and Eliphalet” — the older form of the name."

"“Shalt call me no more Baali” — a word given up to an idol."
